In the 380s, Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, answered practical questions put to him: “Question I. A boy of seven, or a man, who is a catechumen may be present at the offering and eat of it in ignorance. What should be done? Answer. Let him be illuminated, that is, baptized, for he is called by God. ... Question VIII. Should a woman who has just given birth keep the Paschal fast? Answer. No. ... Question X. Is a sick man required to keep the Paschal fast? Answer. No. Question XI. A clergyman is called to celebrate a marriage, and he has heard that it is incestuous. Should he comply and perform the offering? Answer. No; he must not share in other men's sins.”

Our record holds one teacher's sermon on wealth, and Clement gave it in Quis Dives Salvetur: “Consider someone who holds possessions - gold, silver, houses - as gifts of God. From them he serves the God who gives them, for the salvation of others. He knows he owns them more for the sake of his fellow believers than for his own. He is master of what he owns, not a slave to the things he owns. He does not carry them around in his soul. He does not bind his life within them or fence it in. Instead, he is always at work on some good and divine task. One day he may be forced to lose them. Even then, he can bear their loss with a cheerful mind, just as he bears their abundance. This is the one the Lord blesses, the one called poor in spirit. He is a fit heir of the kingdom of heaven, not one who could not live rich.”

Eusebius of Caesarea reported in Church History VI.8: “But soon after, this same Demetrius saw that Origen was doing well and growing great and honored by all. Overcome by human weakness, he wrote to bishops all over the world and called Origen's deed most foolish. But the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem, the most notable and respected bishops in Palestine, judged Origen fully worthy of the honor. They ordained him a presbyter. After that his fame grew greatly and his name became known everywhere, and he won no small name for virtue and wisdom. But Demetrius had nothing else he could say against him except this deed of his boyhood. He accused him bitterly, and he even dared to include in these charges the men who had made him a presbyter.”
